content.title: About
content.content: Kiwi is a small edible fruit of the Actinidia deliciosa vine, native to China. The green variety has a smooth, slightly fuzzy skin and bright‑green flesh dotted with tiny black seeds. The fruit is usually eaten fresh after the skin is removed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kiwi is sometimes called the “Chinese gooseberry,” though its taste is closer to a berry than a pear.
It contains 2–3 times more vitamin C than an orange.
Kiwi provides the enzyme actinidin, which helps break down proteins.
In traditional Chinese medicine kiwi was used to aid digestion.
A golden kiwi with yellow flesh exists, but it is less common in markets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, adds satiety, and supports gut health.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Provides vitamin K and folate
items.content: These nutrients are important for blood clotting and normal cell development.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Kiwi contains polyphenols and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to kiwi, including swelling of the lips and throat.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Kiwi’s high vitamin K content can enhance the effect of certain anticoagulants.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The fruit’s acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kiwi is typically peeled and eaten fresh, added to salads, smoothies, yogurts, desserts, or used in baking. Sliced rounds can be frozen for homemade ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kiwi in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer. Ripe fruits keep 3–5 days, while unripe ones last up to a week until they soften. Keep away from other fruits that trigger rapid ripening.
